title: Article Two

jokes.text: The Pawnee Charter mandates dumping a man named Ted into the lake because the founding fathers' handwriting made 'tea' look like 'ted'
jokes.setup: The town is celebrating 'Ted Party Day,' a seemingly patriotic tradition commemorating the Pawnee tea dump of 1817
jokes.punchline: The entire tradition is based on a handwriting error — 'tea' was misread as 'Ted,' so every year they find a man named Ted and throw him in a lake
jokes.explanation: An exceptional cold open joke that captures the entire spirit of Pawnee in one absurd premise. The joke is original, tightly constructed, and deeply character-integrated — only Pawnee could have this tradition. The reveal that the whole ceremony is a clerical error is perfectly timed and the execution (counting down while the man protests) layers physical comedy on top of the absurdist premise. Strong 8+ because it's genuinely inventive world-building comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Instead of dumping tea in the harbor, they dump a random guy named Ted in the lake.

jokes.text: Ted protests being dumped: 'I don't even go by Ted! I go by Theodore!'
jokes.setup: Ted is being counted down for the lake dunking and protests that he's done with Ted Party Day
jokes.punchline: His only objection to the tradition is the name technicality — he goes by Theodore, not Ted — implying he might accept it otherwise
jokes.explanation: A crisp one-liner that gets a solid laugh through misdirection — we expect a broader protest but the specificity of 'I go by Theodore' is perfectly timed and economical. The implication that the name technicality is somehow his main argument adds a layer of absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The entire tradition is based on a typo

jokes.text: 'That's the way it's always been done' is not a good reason to keep doing something
jokes.setup: Leslie defends Ted Party Day by saying 'That's the way it's always been done'
jokes.punchline: Ted, the victim of the tradition, uses Leslie's own progressive rhetoric against her to argue against it
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — Ted turning Leslie's own logic against her works because it forces her into a hypocritical position. The character integration is good because it plays on Leslie's usually progressive instincts being overridden by her love of Pawnee tradition.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, it's okay Ted. Look, I'm gonna help you dry off. Here, use my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Thanks Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh no wait, here's a photo of you falling into the fountain last year. And here's one of you slipping on the ice. Oh! And here's a video of you getting hit in the face with a pie.

jokes.text: Leslie takes Ted's keys and gives him a quarter: 'I own your car now. The Pawnee Charter clearly states any white citizen has the right to seize any Indian property for 25 cents.'
jokes.setup: Ted challenges Leslie that if they're enforcing every old law, some of them are absurd
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately demonstrates his point by invoking a horrifyingly racist charter provision — then, when called out, echoes his own earlier argument back at him
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-layered joke. First it demonstrates Ted's argument more brutally than he intended. Then Leslie pirouettes and uses his exact words ('we should be careful when we speculate what the Founders intended') against him. The structural mirror is beautifully crafted, the dark subject matter is handled through absurdist distance rather than exploitation, and it's entirely character-specific to Leslie's manic debate style. Justifiably scores 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: There are multiple Teds who all get dumped annually

jokes.text: Ted: 'That is an outdated and racist law. And obviously they meant American Indian.' Leslie: 'Whoa, I think we should be careful when we speculate what the Founders intended when they wrote the charter.'
jokes.setup: Ted earlier used the originalist argument; Leslie used it back at him about the tea/Ted typo
jokes.punchline: Leslie now uses Ted's exact originalist phrasing to defend a racist law, quoting him back to himself perfectly
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural comedy. The callback is precisely deployed — Leslie uses Ted's exact words to defend a position he finds indefensible. It's a logical trap sprung with perfect economy. The joke also functions as sharp political satire about originalism without being preachy. Ted's acknowledgment ('I know what you're doing') makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: There's actually an ordinance from 1952 that says you can purchase any vehicle in Pawnee for a quarter.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not a real law.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: It is. It's right here. 'Any Negro can sell their automobile to a white citizen for twenty-five cents.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: So technically, I could buy your car for a quarter.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, you cannot.

jokes.text: Leslie raises her voice to a landowning male, and per an 1868 statute, he gets to... [slap sound effect implied]
jokes.setup: The back-and-forth about old laws is escalating; Ted has just been rhetorically beaten by Leslie quoting him back
jokes.punchline: Ted invokes an 1868 statute about women raising their voice — implying he's just slapped Leslie — followed by her deadpan 'I was not aware of that statute'
jokes.explanation: The physical gag is implied but lands hard. The escalation of the 'absurd old laws' bit reaches its peak here with a moment that shocks before transitioning to Leslie's perfectly deadpan response. The economy is exceptional — the 1868 date detail makes the joke feel specific and earned. Strong moment of escalation comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Actually, I've been looking into some of our municipal codes, and some of them are quite outdated. For instance, there's a law on the books from 1952 that states... well, it's actually pretty offensive. I probably shouldn't even read it aloud.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ted, come on. We're trying to modernize Pawnee. What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. It says, 'No person of the Oriental persuasion shall operate a business on the east side of Main Street without written consent from the town council.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, that explains a lot.

jokes.text: Leslie's deadpan: 'I was not aware of that statute.'
jokes.setup: Ted has apparently just invoked an 1868 law allowing him to physically retaliate against Leslie
jokes.punchline: Rather than outrage, Leslie's only response is that she was uninformed of this particular statute — perfect Parks-and-Rec character beat
jokes.explanation: This is the true punchline to the previous bit, and it's possibly the best line-reading joke in the scene. Only Leslie Knope would respond to being slapped by lamenting a gap in her legal knowledge. The character integration is near-perfect — this is exactly who she is. Short, devastating, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Well, actually, you said the same thing about how it's pronounced 'tea,' not 'Ted.' So maybe you should listen to what people are saying instead of just waiting for your turn to talk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's not the same thing at all.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Normally, if given a choice between doing something and nothing, I'd choose to do nothing. But I will do something if it helps someone else do nothing. I'd work all night if it meant nothing got done.'
jokes.setup: April asks Ron to get her out of Chris's management training seminar
jokes.punchline: Ron's philosophical statement about productive inaction escalates into a mission statement of anti-government absurdism: working all night so nothing gets done
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ron Swanson lines in the episode. The triple structure ('something'/'nothing'/'nothing got done') builds beautifully, each iteration more absurd and revealing than the last. It's quintessential Ron — not just lazy, but philosophically committed to productive inaction. The escalation to 'I'd work all night if it meant nothing got done' is the kind of line that gets quoted out of context and still lands. Absolutely justifies 8+ — comparable to the calibration anchors in its economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Well, according to an 1887 ordinance, a man is legally permitted to slap a woman if she nags him about his work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ted, that is not a real law.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, the statute is there. I'm not saying I agree with it.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Ron, you've never been CTMTSed?'
jokes.setup: Ron reveals he's never had any management training in 12 years as department head
jokes.punchline: Chris coins 'CTMTSed' as a verb — the absurdity of treating a bureaucratic acronym as a past-tense action verb is peak Chris Traeger
jokes.explanation: A solid character moment — Chris's bureaucratic enthusiasm manifesting as treating his own seminar name like a proper verb is very on-brand. Not a standout joke but genuinely funny in context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to file a complaint with the Parks Department about this incident.

jokes.text: Chris: 'And spoiler alert... It's you. It's ALF.'
jokes.setup: Chris announces that April will have a classmate at the seminar, builds to a reveal
jokes.punchline: He says 'It's you' to Ron — then immediately and nonsensically adds 'It's ALF,' completely deflating any drama
jokes.explanation: The 'It's ALF' non-sequitur is a perfect Chris Traeger absurdist beat — he builds a dramatic reveal and then ruins it with a random 80s sitcom reference, which is funnier than any intentional punchline. Good character-specific comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He'll work hard specifically to accomplish nothing

jokes.text: Ron (talking head): 'I've been head of the Parks Department for 12 years, and I never had any management training course.' / Chris: 'Ron, you've never been CTMTSed?' / Ron: 'This went poorly.'
jokes.setup: Ron smugly argues April doesn't need Chris's seminar since he never had one
jokes.punchline: Ron's talking head cuts to him being cornered — 'This went poorly' — a masterclass in deadpan self-assessment
jokes.explanation: Ron's talking-head 'This went poorly' is a perfect three-word joke — economy at its finest. His total emotional flat-lining in the face of his own miscalculation is exactly who Ron is, and it lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Spoiler alert!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ron's classmate from high school is... Alf!

jokes.text: Ben lists Leslie's custom anniversaries: 'Zoo Day,' 'Double Date Day,' 'Daniel Day-Lewis Day,' 'Talk Like A Pirate Day,' 'Talk Like A Pittsburgh Pirate Day — which, why and how?'
jokes.setup: Ben explains that Leslie has anniversaries for everything and he needs to buy a gift
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from plausible to absurd, culminating in 'Talk Like A Pittsburgh Pirate Day' — the specificity of a struggling MLB team as a holiday subject, punctuated by Ben's baffled 'why and how?', is the peak
jokes.explanation: An excellent list joke with perfect escalation. Each entry is funnier than the last, with 'Daniel Day-Lewis Day' being a great left turn and 'Talk Like A Pittsburgh Pirate Day' being the perfect closer — the Pittsburgh Pirates being a historically terrible team makes the specificity funnier. Ben's 'why and how?' sells the absurdity without over-explaining. Strong character integration: this joke only works because it's Leslie Knope's obsessive love of ritual meeting Ben's exhausted-but-loving-it personality. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What are you bidding on?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I don't know, some weird celebrity memorabilia. It says here it's a signed photo of Fabio with a handwritten note that says 'Stay strong.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's amazing. I'm bidding on a used elliptical machine that Ashton Kutcher allegedly sat on once.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How is that even a thing?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Welcome to high-end charity auctions, Ann.

jokes.text: Ben: 'This calendar was last year's Calendar Day present celebrating the first time she ever bought me a calendar.'
jokes.setup: Ben shows Tom a detailed holiday calendar Leslie made
jokes.punchline: The meta-recursion — a calendar tracking anniversaries, itself given as a 'Calendar Day' gift — perfectly encapsulates Leslie's exponentially expanding holiday universe
jokes.explanation: The recursive absurdity of 'Calendar Day' — a holiday celebrating the gift of a calendar, itself delivered via calendar — is a beautifully constructed joke. It's efficient, character-specific to Leslie's compulsive gift-giving, and the self-referential structure gives it an almost mathematical elegance. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My accountant has specific warnings about my spending.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Like, he'll call me up and say, 'Tom, you can't buy a solid gold toilet seat.' And I'm like, 'But what if I need to?' He's like, 'You don't.' I'm like, 'Okay, but what if society collapses and I need to barter with a gold toilet seat?' He's like, 'That won't happen.' I'm like, 'Your lack of imagination is not my financial problem.'

jokes.text: Ben: 'She always tells me not to, but then she buys me something that's awesome and thoughtful, and then I feel terrible.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks if Ben has to buy a present for every one of Leslie's holidays
jokes.punchline: Ben describes the perfect trap of Leslie's thoughtfulness — being told not to, then being made to feel awful by her amazing gift
jokes.explanation: A relatable relationship observation elevated by being specifically about Leslie. The recognition factor is high — the 'say you don't need anything, then give a perfect gift' trap is universal but lands here because of character context.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie has created so many anniversary days. We have the day we met, the day we first kissed, the day we first said 'I love you,' the day we first held hands, the day we first made eye contact...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was a meaningful glance.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The day we first texted, the day we first emailed, the day we first Instagrammed together, the day we first Snapchatted...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And today is Pirates Day.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Pittsburgh Pirates Day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Not just pirates, but specifically the Pittsburgh Pirates baseball team.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Tyrion Lannister? Lord of Casterly Rock? The Half-Man? You don't watch Game of Thrones?' / Ben: 'No.' / Tom: 'You do?' / Tom: 'Hell yeah. Have you seen those Dothraki dudes? They can get it. Everybody on that show can get it.'
jokes.setup: Ben doesn't know who Tyrion Lannister is; Tom is incredulous, rattles off the character's full titles
jokes.punchline: Tom's encyclopedic Game of Thrones knowledge culminates not in plot analysis but in lustful appreciation of the Dothraki — 'They can get it. Everybody on that show can get it.' Complete tonal pivot from lore-nerd to admirer
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: first the subversion of expecting Tom to NOT be a GoT nerd, and then the bigger subversion of his GoT appreciation being purely physical attraction. 'They can get it' is a highly quotable punchline that perfectly captures Tom's character — even his nerd knowledge is filtered through his libido. Strong character integration: this joke could only be Tom Haverford.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: She has an anniversary for buying him a calendar, celebrated with a calendar

jokes.text: Leslie announces the laws being repealed, including: 'all menstruating women shall be confined to their bathtubs'
jokes.setup: Leslie presents her bill to repeal outdated Pawnee charter laws
jokes.punchline: Among the 110 obsolete laws she lists this specific one — the bathtub confinement law — as the representative example of Pawnee's embarrassing past
jokes.explanation: A competent joke in the show's tradition of absurd Pawnee history. The specificity of 'bathtubs' elevates it slightly above a generic sexist-old-law joke, but it's not as inventive as the charter bits earlier in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I watch Game of Thrones. Those men are fine. Fine!

jokes.text: Garth invokes the citizen filibuster citing 'Article Seven, Section Three' — which Leslie points out defines buffalo meat as acceptable currency
jokes.setup: Garth stands up to filibuster Leslie's bill, citing a specific charter article and section
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately knows that section is the 'buffalo meat as acceptable currency' provision — not a filibuster rule at all. Garth corrects himself
jokes.explanation: A nicely constructed bit — Leslie's instant recall of the buffalo meat provision while Garth fumbles his own citation reveals both characters perfectly. Leslie's encyclopedic charter knowledge (her thing) intersects with Garth's fanaticism. The 'buffalo meat as acceptable currency' detail is a good absurdist Pawnee world-building beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie is always doing these thoughtful things, and it's exhausting because then I feel guilty for not reciprocating immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, who has time to be that considerate? It's like a full-time job.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? That came out wrong. Leslie, I'm sorry. I love that you're thoughtful. I'm the worst.

jokes.text: Garth begins his filibuster by sharing 'some ideas I have for J.J. Abrams' seventh chapter in the Star Wars Saga' — including Boba Fett escaping the Sarlacc pit
jokes.setup: Having established his filibuster rights, Garth begins his time-filling content
jokes.punchline: Rather than a political speech, he launches into a detailed, earnest Star Wars fan theory — complete with blocking and cinematography suggestions
jokes.explanation: Garth is immediately established as a magnificent type — the passionate civic obstruction nerd who channels his energy into fandom. The Boba Fett Sarlacc pit escape was a real fan theory at the time, making this feel authentic rather than random. The joke has good legs because it keeps going.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you just said, but I love you.

jokes.text: Garth: 'After a beat, Luke says, "Darth Vader was my father, but Ben Kenobi was my master." And he cuts Hannibal Lecter in half.'
jokes.setup: The Star Wars filibuster continues with increasingly bizarre crossover content
jokes.punchline: The filibuster peaks with Hannibal Lecter inexplicably appearing in a Star Wars/Marvel crossover and being cut in half by Luke Skywalker
jokes.explanation: The escalation lands perfectly here — we've gone from Star Wars to Marvel to now Hannibal Lecter, and the jump is so unexpected it's genuinely funny. 'He cuts Hannibal Lecter in half' delivered as a matter-of-fact plot beat is a great absurdist punchline. The economy is strong — Hannibal Lecter appearing with no setup or explanation is the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Garth Gripling
dialogue.line: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak about a matter of great importance to this body, nay, to this nation. And I have prepared some remarks that I believe will illuminate the path forward for all of us gathered here. Now, I've taken the liberty of writing what I call 'Twilight: New Moon: A Pawnee Remix,' where Bella Swan is actually the Deputy Director of Parks and Recreation, and Edward Cullen is a emotionally unavailable city planner, and—

jokes.text: Garth: 'You can't just change the charter willy-nilly. You start by casually repealing a couple old laws, next thing you know your jackbooted Stormtroopers are kicking in my door... if I were married.'
jokes.setup: Garth makes a slippery-slope argument about changing the charter
jokes.punchline: His dramatic rant about jackbooted Stormtroopers is immediately undercut by the parenthetical 'if I were married' — the self-aware lonely bachelor admission punctures his own dramatic speech
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured joke — Garth builds to an impassioned political statement, then deflates it entirely with 'if I were married.' The economy is outstanding: three words completely recontextualize everything before them. It simultaneously characterizes Garth (the passionate loner) and gets a huge laugh from the abrupt pivot to pathos. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: Robot Chewbacca delivered with complete confidence

jokes.text: Garth: 'Oh, big deal, you put on a costume for a couple hours.' / Leslie: 'By that logic, every time I go to bed at night, I am Wolverine.'
jokes.setup: Leslie defends her Pawnee Historical House experience; Garth dismisses it as costume-wearing
jokes.punchline: Leslie's Wolverine reveal — she goes to bed in X-Men pajamas — is unexpected and perfectly silly
jokes.explanation: A standout line — the Wolverine punchline is completely unexpected given the political context of the argument. It works because Leslie uses airtight logical structure (correctly!) to arrive at an absurd conclusion. The joke also sets up the follow-through about how Garth got his pajamas, making the whole exchange a two-part gem. 'Every time I go to bed at night, I am Wolverine' is highly quotable, character-specific, and funny on its own outside context. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: Just because you own something doesn't make you an expert on it. I own X-Men pajamas, but that doesn't make me an expert on the X-Men.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I think it kind of does.

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: No, it really doesn't.

jokes.text: Garth: 'You bought X-Men pajamas?' / Leslie: 'I won them, madam, in a raffle.'
jokes.setup: Garth is surprised Leslie has X-Men pajamas
jokes.punchline: 'I won them, madam, in a raffle' — the archaic 'madam,' the specificity of winning them (not buying), and Leslie's total dignity in this admission all compound
jokes.explanation: 'I won them, madam, in a raffle' is near-perfect comedy writing. Every word is load-bearing: 'won' (not bought, implying a different kind of relationship with the pajamas), 'madam' (hilariously formal and slightly offended dignity), 'in a raffle' (the specific delivery mechanism adds absurdist texture). It's the ideal button to the Wolverine joke. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why are you wearing pajamas?

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: I won them in a raffle.

jokes.text: Leslie: '...they also had wooden teeth and pooped in holes in the ground. It was a more primitive time.' / Garth: 'It was a better time.'
jokes.setup: Leslie argues the Founders were brilliant but primitive; Garth challenges her
jokes.punchline: Garth's flat counter — 'It was a better time' — in response to 'pooped in holes in the ground' is a perfect character-defining absurdist statement
jokes.explanation: A clean, efficient joke that works because of Garth's utter conviction. 'Pooped in holes in the ground' is a great setup and 'It was a better time' is a minimal, maximally committed reply. Strong Garth characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, the founders weren't perfect. They owned slaves, they didn't let women vote, and some of them thought Native Americans were basically just obstacles.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But you know what? They still created a system where we could fix those things. That's the real genius.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Hop on board The Management Train. First stop, Motivation Station. All aboard!'
jokes.setup: The CTMTS seminar begins with Ron and April as reluctant participants
jokes.punchline: Chris's unironic, full-enthusiasm 'Management Train' metaphor — complete with 'All aboard!' — in front of two people who clearly hate everything about this
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe-comedy beat. Chris's irrepressible corporate-cheerleader energy playing against Ron's disgust is a reliable Parks dynamic. Not exceptional but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Good morning everyone! Today we're going to talk about leadership, and I want you to think of your department like a train. You're the conductor, and your employees are the passengers. Now, some people say you should be a servant leader, but I say you should be a *locomotive* leader! You need to build momentum, you need to keep on the tracks, and most importantly, you need to make sure everyone on board is moving at the same velocity toward our corporate synergy destination!

jokes.text: Ben to Ann on the waffle iron auction: 'Stop bidding on my waffle iron. You're "Future Mrs. Tiger Woods"?' / Ann: 'I made that profile, like, ten years ago. I don't know how to change it.'
jokes.setup: Ben realizes he's been outbid by someone named 'Future Mrs. Tiger Woods'
jokes.punchline: The profile name reveals Ann made it during Tiger Woods' peak fame and hasn't updated it — charming, slightly embarrassing self-revelation
jokes.explanation: A nice character beat for Ann — slightly embarrassing but endearing. The Tiger Woods reference has a specific datedness that works in context (though it dates the episode).

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, your eBay username is 'FitMom2024'?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I made that account in 2015.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you've been 'FitMom2024' for nine years?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I thought I'd be fit by then. And a mom. I was very optimistic.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Mine's in June.' [reveals she also has a Waffle Day for Leslie]
jokes.setup: Ben explains he's trying to win the waffle iron for Leslie's Breakfast Day
jokes.punchline: Ann reveals she's also competing for it — for Leslie's Waffle Day in June — establishing Leslie has separate but equivalent food-based breakfast holidays with different people
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Ann has her own parallel breakfast holiday with Leslie is a great escalation of the anniversaries bit. 'Mine's in June' — delivered with equal parts pride and exhaustion — perfectly mirrors Ben's situation and deepens the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Being married to Leslie is like being hit over the head with a golf club made of love and kindness.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I can't believe I'm complaining about how thoughtful my wife is. I'm sorry, honey. I love you.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann are bonding over the exhaustion of Leslie's anniversary demands
jokes.punchline: Ben catches himself complaining about Leslie's thoughtfulness and immediately apologizes directly to the camera/her, breaking the commiseration
jokes.explanation: A sweet character moment that functions as a mild joke — Ben's self-correction is endearing and gets a soft laugh. It's more warm than funny but works in the show's register.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A locomotive is a large piece of machinery. It doesn't think or feel. It just moves forward with no regard for what's in its way. That's not a metaphor I appreciate.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Oh, God. We've lost the auction.' / Ann: 'What?' / Ben: 'Somebody swooped in at the last second...' / Ann: 'Okay, Tyrion Lannister, why don't you just cast a spell and get us the waffle iron back?' / Ben (long-suffering): 'Okay. I don't even have time to tell you how wrong you are. Actually, it's gonna bug me if I don't. The Lannisters, while very wealthy, do not possess the magical abilities of, say, the Warlocks of Qarth.'
jokes.setup: They lose the auction; Ann sarcastically references Tyrion Lannister
jokes.punchline: Ben cannot let the GoT inaccuracy slide even in a moment of crisis — his compulsive correction about Lannister vs. Warlock magical abilities is a perfect nerd character beat
jokes.explanation: The 'Warlocks of Qarth' correction is Ben Wyatt at his most character-specific. The joke is constructed beautifully: 'I don't even have time... actually it's gonna bug me if I don't' sets up the compulsion before delivering the deeply specific lore correction. The specificity of 'Warlocks of Qarth' (a real show detail) elevates this above generic nerd humor. 'This is why we don't hang out' is the perfect button. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, in Game of Thrones, they don't cast spells. That's more of a Harry Potter thing. Game of Thrones has magic, but it's much more subtle and mysterious.

jokes.text: Ron: 'First of all, you don't steer a locomotive. The tracks do. Second, there are only three ways to motivate people. Money, fear, and hunger.'
jokes.setup: Chris asks them to think of themselves as engineers 'steering a locomotive of positivity'
jokes.punchline: Ron dismantles the metaphor with literal accuracy first, then pivots to his actual motivational philosophy: money, fear, and hunger
jokes.explanation: A masterful Ron Swanson line. The literal-minded attack on Chris's metaphor ('you don't steer a locomotive, the tracks do') is both funny and correct, establishing Ron's character. Then 'money, fear, and hunger' as the complete list of human motivators is a perfectly compressed statement of Swanson philosophy. Quotability is extremely high — 'money, fear, and hunger' functions as a standalone Ron Swanson quote. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You don't steer a locomotive. You operate the throttle and engage the brake system.

jokes.text: Chris: 'When people feel supported, they will literally explode with productivity.'
jokes.setup: Ron lists money/fear/hunger; Chris counters with encouragement and smiles
jokes.punchline: Chris's use of 'literally explode' as enthusiastic hyperbole — a verbal tic that the show has established — is gently absurd
jokes.explanation: A running gag on Chris's 'literally' hyperbole. It's reliable but not exceptional — functions as a character tag more than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: There are three ways to motivate people: money, fear, and women.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Interestingly, a woman can be used to motivate a man, but money and fear don't work on women.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And a woman can be motivated by money, but not fear or another woman.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: As for a third woman, it's complicated.

jokes.text: Chris: 'What about encouragement, appreciation, and smiles. When people feel supported, they will literally explode with productivity.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just listed money, fear, and hunger as the only motivators
jokes.punchline: Chris counters with 'smiles' as a motivational tool, then uses 'literally explode with productivity' — a malaprop that undermines his case
jokes.explanation: Decent Chris character beat. 'Literally explode with productivity' is a nice misuse of 'literally' that's very Chris-specific. Functional contrast to Ron's prior line.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: As a manager, I literally have to be a thousand different people every single day.

jokes.text: April: 'Can you guys just figure out which way is better and tell me so we can leave?'
jokes.setup: Ron and Chris are engaged in a philosophical debate about motivation theory
jokes.punchline: April cuts through all of it with pure pragmatic nihilism — she doesn't care about the debate, she just wants to leave
jokes.explanation: Classic April — her complete disengagement from the debate expressed as a practical request ('just tell me so we can leave') is sharp and efficient. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Chris killed my spirit. He murdered it. There's spirit blood all over this office and nobody cares.

jokes.text: April: 'You're not being very inclusive, Chris. I feel like my input isn't being appreciated. You've killed my spirit. My spirit blood is on your hands.'
jokes.setup: Chris ignores April's suggestion to end the seminar, citing the syllabus
jokes.punchline: April weaponizes Chris's own management philosophy against him — using the language of supportive management ('inclusive,' 'appreciated') to accuse him of murder, culminating in 'spirit blood'
jokes.explanation: April turns Chris's management philosophy into a weapon against him with perfect comedic escalation. 'My spirit blood is on your hands' is a brilliant dark-absurdist punchline — the logical endpoint of taking corporate wellness language to its extreme conclusion. The joke is deeply character-specific to April's gothic irony and her ability to turn sincerity into weaponized absurdism. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This house is old. It smells like old. The floors are old, the walls are old, everything is old. You know what the solution is? We just need to make it new.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How? Simple. We tear it down and build a Applebee's.

jokes.text: Chris (talking head): 'My God, I've taught you so much already.'
jokes.setup: April has just weaponized his own positive management language against him
jokes.punchline: Chris interprets April's manipulation as genuine learning — he's been completely fooled and is delighted about it
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to April's manipulation scene. Chris's complete misreading of the situation is both funny and character-specific — his relentless optimism makes him impervious to sarcasm. The irony is rich.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm a referee because I have nothing better to do.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm a referee because I have way better things to do, and this is one of them.

jokes.text: Ron talking head: 'I don't want to seem overdramatic, but this is literally a battle for April's soul.' / Chris talking head: 'I don't want to seem overdramatic, but I don't really care what happens here.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Chris are framed as competing forces in a challenge to motivate workers
jokes.punchline: Ron uses 'I don't want to seem overdramatic' to introduce a genuinely dramatic statement; Chris uses the exact same preface to introduce complete apathy — perfect character contrast
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant parallel construction that perfectly encapsulates both characters simultaneously. Ron's dramatic investment in April's soul versus Chris's cheerful indifference to the outcome — both prefaced with the same phrase — is comedic writing at a high level. The mirror structure means each line makes the other funnier. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have the advantage of not having a Victorian disease. I mean, sure, I have a lot of problems, but none of them are cholera or whatever.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I don't know, Tom. I think there's some pretty cool things from back then. That is a dope bonnet.'
jokes.setup: Tom complains that the historical house is old and dumb; Andy seems to genuinely enjoy it
jokes.punchline: Wait — Tom is talking to himself, playing both sides of the conversation ('I don't know, Tom') while simultaneously complimenting an 1817 bonnet as 'dope'
jokes.explanation: Tom addressing himself in conversation ('I don't know, Tom') while using contemporary slang to describe 1817 fashion ('dope bonnet') is a good character-specific bit. The self-address detail is the sharper comedic element.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me that even the mailwoman has a specific anniversary with Leslie?

dialogue.speaker: Roz
dialogue.line: Every first Tuesday of the month. She brings her a waffle.

jokes.text: Garth has already done the preserves and 'chased off an interloping cable installer' — having slept in the historical house overnight
jokes.setup: Leslie and Garth set up the living-in-the-historical-house challenge
jokes.punchline: Garth has already been there overnight and is fully committed to the 1817 lifestyle, having chased off a cable installer as though he were an interloper from the future
jokes.explanation: The 'interloping cable installer' detail is a great Garth character beat — he's treating 1817 method-acting with complete seriousness. Good world-building joke for the character.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnshop owner
dialogue.line: I'll give you fifty bucks for that kidney.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: ...Do you take payment plans?

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Antiperspirant? Not allowed. Might get a little rough in there.'
jokes.setup: Leslie continues her preparation checklist for 1817 living
jokes.punchline: The masterful understatement: no antiperspirant in a period house with butter-churning and physical labor = 'Might get a little rough in there'
jokes.explanation: A functional understatement joke that follows nicely from 'Rickets? Cured' but isn't as strong. Gets a mild laugh on the understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This historical challenge is impossible. You know what? I'm just going to unplug it and plug it back in.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If that doesn't work, I'm going to throw it in the river.

jokes.text: Roz the mailwoman appears to also want the waffle iron — for 'Mail Day,' the anniversary of the first time she delivered Leslie's mail
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann are in a bidding war over the waffle iron with the original 'Tall Tyrion Lannister' bidder
jokes.punchline: A third competitor appears — Leslie's mailwoman — who has her own independent anniversary holiday with Leslie, 'Mail Day,' extending the absurdity of Leslie's relationship-anniversary universe
jokes.explanation: The appearance of Leslie's mailwoman as a waffle iron competitor is a great escalation of the anniversary bit. It transforms the joke from 'Leslie is excessive with her close friends' to 'Leslie forms intense commemorative bonds with everyone she meets.' The structural escalation is well-executed, and 'Roz' being a complete stranger to the audience makes the reveal land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Butter on popcorn, butter on toast, butter on waffles, butter on... grapes?

jokes.text: Pawn shop owner: 'Let's start the bidding at $650,000.' / Ben: 'I'll counter with 100 bucks.'
jokes.setup: Three-way bidding war breaks out over the waffle iron
jokes.punchline: The pawn shop owner opens at $650,000 for a used waffle iron; Ben immediately counters with $100, completely ignoring the gap
jokes.explanation: A solid absurdist joke about pawnshop pricing — the gap between $650,000 and $100 is the entire joke. Well-executed but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I love all foods with butter. Buttered popcorn, buttered toast, buttered butter...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, I think butter is my favorite food.

jokes.text: Pawn shop owner to Ann: 'I'll give it to you if you go on a date with me.' / Ann: 'Oh God, I can't believe I'm about to do this, but fine. One date. But let me make one thing perfectly clear...' / Roz: '500 bucks.' / Owner: 'Sold.' / Ann: 'You still want to go out?' / Owner: 'I just come into some money. $500 buys a lot of nitrous.'
jokes.setup: The pawn shop owner offers the waffle iron to Ann in exchange for a date; she reluctantly agrees
jokes.punchline: Roz immediately outbids with $500 — the owner drops Ann for the cash, revealing the date offer was purely transactional. His explanation: '$500 buys a lot of nitrous'
jokes.explanation: A well-structured misdirection sequence: we're set up for Ann's reluctant date humiliation, then the owner immediately abandons the premise for cash, then explains the cash will fund nitrous oxide. Each beat is a surprise. '$500 buys a lot of nitrous' is a strong, weird punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look at this! A hoop! You just roll it with a stick and it goes and goes and goes!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is the best toy ever made. I'm gonna play with this all day.

jokes.text: Garth: 'Yeah, nothing warms the blood like an old whirly-bout with the old butter-gyre, eh, Leslie?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Garth are living in the historical house; he's butter-churning
jokes.punchline: Garth's complete fluency in period-appropriate vernacular (referring to a butter churn as a 'butter-gyre') and his sincere enthusiasm for it ('warms the blood') is the joke
jokes.explanation: A strong Garth character moment — his authentic use of invented/archaic terminology and genuine pleasure in primitive tasks perfectly characterizes him as someone truly built for 1817. 'Nothing warms the blood' is a perfect period register.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Jerry, can you file these folders?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, absolutely! I love filing. And these folders—manila folders, the superior folder—with the metal fasteners. Not the cheap ones, the good ones. And the labels, oh the labels are so crisp and white. I'm gonna organize these so well, Chris. By color, by size, by date, alphabetically, reverse alphabetically. This is the best day of my life.

jokes.text: Tom: 'One time my refrigerator stopped working, I didn't know what to do. I just moved.'
jokes.setup: Tom marvels at how Leslie and Garth are surviving 1817 conditions
jokes.punchline: Tom's solution to a broken refrigerator — moving apartments rather than fixing it — reveals the depth of his helplessness with practical matters
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed Tom Haverford joke. The setup is efficient (can't handle the historical house), and the punchline is unexpected: rather than calling a repairman, Tom MOVED. It's absurd but totally believable for Tom, and the economy is exceptional — the joke takes six words to deliver. High quotability because it's fully autonomous outside context. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Garth has no emails from the last six months. Nothing. Not even spam.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not possible. Everyone gets emails. Unless... he's a ghost.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's not a ghost, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A vampire then. Vampires don't use email. They use the dark web.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'He has that look in his eye that Ben gets when he plays Risk.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is worried that Garth is more committed to the challenge than expected
jokes.punchline: She characterizes Garth's intensity by comparing him to Ben playing Risk — an unexpected, specific, and perfect character insight
jokes.explanation: The Risk comparison is a beautifully specific character beat — it tells us something true about Ben (intense board game player) while efficiently communicating that Garth is dangerously committed. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Garth. I was trying to find evidence that you were cheating on me, but instead I found... nothing. No texts, no calls, no social media.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You don't have a single friend who's texted you in months. Your mother is your most frequent contact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Garth, I came here ready for a fight, but now I'm just... I'm worried about you.

jokes.text: Andy: 'All my favorite foods have butter on 'em. Pancakes, toast, popcorn, grapes.' [beat] 'Butter is my favorite food.'
jokes.setup: Andy is tasting the butter Garth is churning from the butter-gyre
jokes.punchline: Andy lists foods that have butter on them, then reveals that butter itself is his favorite food — the list was a preamble to this realization, and 'grapes' in the buttered-foods list is the earlier absurdist surprise
jokes.explanation: A great Andy Dwyer joke with two laugh beats: 'grapes' in the butter-foods list (unexpected), and then the reveal that butter is his FAVORITE food (the point of the list). The structure is clean and the character integration is excellent — this could only be Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's so lonely he responds to spam

jokes.text: Garth: 'Well, then you're gonna love what I'm churning up.' [reveals the butter product] / Andy and others react in horror: 'Oh, my God. This is horrifying. Nobody eat that.'
jokes.setup: Andy expresses love for butter; Garth invites him to look at what he's churning
jokes.punchline: The butter product is apparently deeply wrong-looking — whatever it is causes immediate horror; the visual gag is implied from the reactions
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that depends entirely on the image — the horror reactions sell it but without seeing what Garth produced, the transcript version is weaker. On screen this is likely funnier than it reads.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What am I supposed to do with this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, treat it like a cursed object that requires supernatural disposal.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you could try burying it at a crossroads at midnight, or maybe burn it in a sacred fire.

jokes.text: Garth 'brought his own whale blubber to light the lamps' — and appears to be getting stronger over time
jokes.setup: Andy and Tom observe Garth's growing mastery of 1817 living
jokes.punchline: The whale blubber detail establishes that Garth over-prepared for this challenge in a way that reveals fanatical commitment — he didn't just accept the challenge, he came with a whale blubber supply
jokes.explanation: The whale blubber detail is a solid world-building character joke. Garth becoming stronger as the challenge continues ('like he's getting stronger the longer he stays here') is a good escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Jerry, you're useless. You'll never amount to anything. Now get back to work.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yes, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wow, Ron, that's really harsh. But I have to admit... Jerry's been incredibly productive all morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly. Fear is the most effective motivator.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to try that with my interns.

jokes.text: Garth rolls a hoop past the window: 'Wee! Look at my hoop, Leslie! Look at my hoop!'
jokes.setup: Leslie and others are struggling with 1817 living while Garth thrives
jokes.punchline: Garth rolls a hoop (an 1817 toy) with genuine glee, screaming at Leslie to watch — his childlike joy in primitive recreation while others suffer is a perfect character beat
jokes.explanation: A great physical comedy beat — Garth's hoop-rolling joy is the perfect visual manifestation of his 1817 contentment. 'Look at my hoop, Leslie! Look at my hoop!' is highly quotable because of the unironic enthusiasm. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What are you whittling?

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: A bloodletting lance. It's an ominous historical medical implement.

jokes.text: Leslie talking head: 'It's fun to be here on, like, a school field trip or something. It's so, so, so fun. So, so fun. But to live like this is insane.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is struggling with the historical house challenge
jokes.punchline: Her talking head swings between over-qualified enthusiasm ('so, so, so fun') and absolute clarity ('to live like this is insane') — the tension between her public-servant cheerfulness and private honesty
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat — Leslie's forced enthusiasm before admitting defeat is relatable and character-specific. Not exceptional but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so we're starting a new Ted tradition?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm Ted now.

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: No, I'm Ted.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm definitely Ted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You can't all be Ted!

dialogue.speaker: Garth
dialogue.line: We're all Ted.

jokes.text: Andy/Leslie: 'There's no way a man who's into X-Men that much can stay away from the Internet that long. We should check his phone.'
jokes.setup: Leslie suspects Garth must be cheating to last this long without technology
jokes.punchline: Her evidence is his X-Men fandom — establishing that being THIS into X-Men requires constant Internet access, which is a specific and funny modern observation
jokes.explanation: A callback to the X-Men pajama joke that works as both a character callback and a contemporary observation about fandom requiring Internet access. Good structural connection but not exceptional as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, let's celebrate Ted for all his hard work!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah! Ted's the best! Woo!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Celebrating! Ted deserves it!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Everybody celebrate with me!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, put your clothes back on!

jokes.text: Ron to Jerry: 'This is the top priority. I need these blue folders done now. You can eat when you have finished. File!'
jokes.setup: Ron is testing his 'fear and hunger' motivational method on Jerry as counter-experiment
jokes.punchline: Ron withholding food from Jerry ('you can eat when you have finished') and barking 'File!' is Ron's philosophy literally applied — it's both funny and slightly horrifying
jokes.explanation: Ron's three-word command 'File!' and withholding of food is a great extension of his motivational philosophy to its logical (horrible) conclusion. The dark subversive element — treating an employee like a dog — is played entirely straight, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron and Chris are competing to see who's the better manager. Two men enter, one man leaves. But honestly, I'm just hoping they both lose and I get to be manager.

jokes.text: Ron talking head: 'Money, fear, hunger.' [delivered with complete satisfaction after watching his method work]
jokes.setup: Ron has made Jerry file under duress; the experiment appears to be working
jokes.punchline: Ron repeating 'Money, fear, hunger' as a satisfied conclusion — a callback to his earlier statement, now functioning as triumphant proof of his philosophy
jokes.explanation: The callback works beautifully — the three-word philosophy functions as both setup and punchline, and hearing it again as triumphant confirmation is satisfying. Three words, maximum impact. The callback structure elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My detailed plan to manipulate the situation and commit petty theft.

jokes.text: Ben and Ann check Garth's phone and discover he hasn't gotten an email in twelve days. Andy: 'Is he a ghost?' / Ann: 'The only ones he gets are spam. And he responds to them.'
jokes.setup: They check Garth's phone to see if he's cheating with the internet
jokes.punchline: Instead of catching a cheater, they discover Garth's deep social isolation — no real emails in 12 days, only spam which he responds to. Andy's 'Is he a ghost?' adds an absurdist layer
jokes.explanation: A beautifully dark joke about loneliness. 'He responds to them' (responding to spam) is genuinely sad and funny simultaneously. Andy's 'Is he a ghost?' is a perfect absurdist beat that lands on top of the pathos. The joke works because it makes you feel slightly bad for Garth while still laughing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She already has a category for joint presents for these specific holidays

jokes.text: Ann: 'I don't know. Seems like he's friends with that mule.'
jokes.setup: 'This guy has no friends' — the group is processing Garth's social isolation
jokes.punchline: Ann finds a silver lining: Garth has a mule friend — delivered as sincere consolation, which makes it darker
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical dark joke. 'Seems like he's friends with that mule' is delivered as genuine consolation, which makes it much funnier than if it were played as a burn. The economy — one sentence, complete dark laugh — is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is our last Breakfast/Waffle Day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why? Are we dying?

jokes.text: Ben's attempt to make a 'miniature Leslie out of breakfast food' as an alternative gift
jokes.setup: Ben can't win the waffle iron and needs an alternative gift
jokes.punchline: His solution is to sculpt a miniature Leslie from breakfast food — the absurdity of the craft project plus the inference that it looks terrible from Ann's visible reaction
jokes.explanation: A solid visual gag concept — the breakfast food Leslie sculpture is funny both as a concept and as a visual (presumably horrifying). Ben's earnest attempt at an artisanal gift is character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so we've agreed on alternating Thanksgivings and splitting Christmas?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, but what about New Year's? I feel like New Year's should be its own thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, we literally just made this compromise five seconds ago.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but New Year's Eve is when all the best parties happen, and I have a tradition of wearing white pants and making a speech about the future, and I would really like Ben to be there for that.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We can work something out with New Year's.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What about Valentine's Day?

jokes.text: Ann's suggestion for what to do with the breakfast-food Leslie sculpture: 'Just burn it and bury the ashes and pray it doesn't haunt you.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks what to do with his failed breakfast-food Leslie sculpture
jokes.punchline: Ann's escalating destruction protocol — burn, bury, pray it doesn't haunt — implies the sculpture is so disturbing it requires spiritual containment
jokes.explanation: An excellently constructed three-part escalation: 'burn it' (normal disposal) → 'bury the ashes' (over-caution) → 'pray it doesn't haunt you' (supernatural threat). The structure is tight, the dark comedy escalates perfectly, and the final beat ('haunt you') is both unexpected and logical given the presumed horror of the food sculpture. Highly quotable standalone line. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron replaces Jerry's red folders with blue ones mid-task: 'You can eat when you have finished. File!'
jokes.setup: Chris has motivated Jerry with positive reinforcement; Ron intervenes to test his own method
jokes.punchline: Ron's Pavlovian experiment — switching folder colors and withholding food — treats Jerry as a test subject, which is funny and grim
jokes.explanation: A running gag extension of the Jerry experiments. Functional but not as punchy as the original setup.

jokes.text: Garth whittles a 'birthing stick.' Andy: 'What's that?' / Garth: 'You do not want to know.' / Andy: 'Oh, my God.'
jokes.setup: Garth is whittling something while Leslie is changing
jokes.punchline: A 'birthing stick' — its purpose deliberately left unexplained but clearly horrifying — combined with Andy's immediate existential reaction
jokes.explanation: Economy is exceptional — 'You do not want to know' tells us everything about what a birthing stick is without telling us anything. The joke works entirely through implication. Andy's 'Oh, my God' reaction seals it. Tightly constructed dark beat.

jokes.text: Leslie concedes by changing clothes. Garth: 'Violation. You are bonnetless!' / Leslie: 'Yes, you're right. I admit, I can't take it anymore. You win.' / Garth: 'Huzzah! The day is mine.' / Garth pause: 'I'm gonna miss saying huzzah.'
jokes.setup: Leslie changes clothes, violating the 1817 rules, effectively conceding the challenge
jokes.punchline: After his triumphant 'Huzzah!', Garth's immediate wistfulness about losing the word 'huzzah' from his vocabulary is a perfect character beat — he'll miss the language more than the victory
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm gonna miss saying huzzah' beat is perfect character comedy. After winning, Garth's emotional focus is on losing access to the word 'huzzah' — it reveals everything about him: the love of the aesthetic, the period authenticity, and the slight sadness of returning to modernity. It also has great quotability and rewatch value because of how sincere it is. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Garth: 'Yes, I will go out on a date with you, but I realize you're a modern woman, so I will let you pay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie makes Garth a new proposition; he misunderstands it as a date invitation
jokes.punchline: Garth's 'modern woman' concession — agreeing to be progressive by letting HER pay — inverts the traditional gallantry while missing the point entirely
jokes.explanation: A clever character inversion — Garth's attempt at progressive accommodation still centers his own preferences. 'I will let you pay' as modern feminism is a good irony beat. Strong Garth characterization.

jokes.text: Garth's complaints about the Historical Commission's newsletter: 'They haven't answered a single one of my complaints about their anachronistic use of fonts.'
jokes.setup: Leslie invites Garth to join the Pawnee Historical Commission
jokes.punchline: Garth refuses by citing a specific grievance about font anachronism in their newsletter — his objection is both deeply specific and entirely in character
jokes.explanation: The 'anachronistic use of fonts' complaint is an excellent character detail — Garth's passion for period authenticity extends to typography. It's specific, believable for this character, and efficiently communicated. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie reverse-psychologies Garth into joining: 'There's tons of meetings, lots of work with people who also love history, and many social occasions... like cocktail parties. I can understand if it's something you don't want to commit to.'
jokes.setup: Garth has refused the Historical Commission invitation
jokes.punchline: Leslie's obvious reverse psychology — describing the Commission's activities in appealing terms while warning him away — is effective and gently funny. Garth immediately starts caving
jokes.explanation: A functional Leslie Knope character beat — her manipulative enthusiasm is a known comedy tool. Not exceptional but serves the scene.

jokes.text: Garth: 'Just sounds like such a big bite out of my soap-making time. My cousin's arraignment is in May. But that's a day. I just fly out, I come back the same day.'
jokes.setup: Garth is weighing the Historical Commission invitation
jokes.punchline: His hesitation concerns his soap-making time and a cousin's arraignment — the casual mention of a family member's arraignment as a scheduling concern (not moral concern) is the dark comedy beat
jokes.explanation: The cousin's arraignment detail is exactly the kind of background character-building joke Parks does well. Garth mentions it with zero emotional weight — it's just a scheduling item — which implies a family history that enriches his eccentricity. Good dark-subversive beat.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'I did not change Article Two, though. I just couldn't vote against a good, old-fashioned lake dunking.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has successfully repealed all outdated laws — the whole point of the episode
jokes.punchline: Despite her progressive mission, she carved out an exception for Ted Party Day — she literally can't vote against a lake dunking. The irony of the progressive lawmaker keeping the most absurd tradition
jokes.explanation: A great ironic callback to the cold open — Leslie's entire arc of progressive legal reform is revealed to have a giant exception for the tradition that started everything. 'I just couldn't vote against a good, old-fashioned lake dunking' perfectly captures Leslie's contradiction of loving both progress and tradition.

jokes.text: The volunteer Ted ceremony: Garth in full historical dress shouts 'Huzzah, I'm Ted! I'm Ted!' — then Andy joins naked: 'He's naked, everybody! Put that away!'
jokes.setup: The compromise: a volunteer Ted will be dunked going forward. Garth volunteers with great ceremony
jokes.punchline: Garth's huzzah-filled enthusiasm is perfect, but Andy showing up naked ('We're all Ted!') escalates it to physical comedy chaos
jokes.explanation: The episode's final set piece lands well because it pays off multiple running elements: Ted Party Day, Garth's character, and Andy's irrepressible chaos energy. Garth's 'Huzzah, I'm Ted!' is perfect — his earlier sentiment about missing 'huzzah' pays off immediately. Andy's naked escalation is a classic Andy beat.

jokes.text: Garth is dunked in the lake as the new volunteer Ted, shouting 'Huzzah, I'm Ted!' while being counted down.
jokes.setup: The Ted Party Day compromise allows a volunteer to be dunked as Ted.
jokes.punchline: Garth, who spent the episode opposing all change to the charter, is now enthusiastically volunteering to be dunked — having been fully co-opted into the tradition he defended.
jokes.explanation: A perfect plot resolution joke. The character who spent the episode protecting tradition from change ends it by joyfully participating in the tradition's updated form — and shouting 'Huzzah, I'm Ted!' while being thrown in a lake. The 'Huzzah' callback is the right button. Strong earned payoff.

jokes.text: Old Ted, post-dunking: 'Thank God. I don't know how to swim.'
jokes.setup: The original Ted watches the volunteer dunking with relief
jokes.punchline: His coda — 'I don't know how to swim' — retroactively makes every previous Ted Party Day potentially lethal, delivered as casual relief rather than horror
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode button — retroactively making all prior Ted dunkings potentially murderous while Ted mentions it with casual relief. The economy is exceptional: five words that reframe the entire cold open. 'Thank God. I don't know how to swim.' is a highly quotable, dark-subversive capper. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: After Andy jumps in naked: 'Thank God. I don't know how to swim.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just jumped into a lake naked with great enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he can't swim — the 'thank God' implies he survived the jump and is relieved, without any apparent awareness of the danger he put himself in
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy Dwyer joke. The structure is excellent: the physical comedy of the naked lake jump is already funny, and then the post-hoc revelation that he can't swim — delivered with relief rather than panic — reframes the whole scene. The 'Thank God' as his opener suggests it occurred to him only after he landed. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: The results of the Jerry experiments are revealed: 'He was so happy when you told him he was doing a great job that he spent 20 minutes on the phone telling Gayle about it.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Chris tabulate Jerry's filing results from their competing motivation experiments
jokes.punchline: Jerry's positive reinforcement was so overwhelming he spent 20 minutes calling his wife — reducing his filing output. His deep starvation for basic workplace validation is both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: The Jerry-Gayle detail is a great character beat — Jerry immediately calls his wife when he gets compliments at work, revealing both his home life happiness and his workplace sadness. Builds on established Jerry character effectively.

jokes.text: Ron: 'He may have filed more blue ones, but they're almost all filed wrong. Not surprising since he was a mess after you talked to him.'
jokes.setup: Chris argues that his positive reinforcement produced more filing (blue folders)
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals the quality was terrible — because Ron's fear/hunger method made Jerry an emotional wreck — leaving neither method vindicated
jokes.explanation: A good structural resolution to the management debate — both methods failed Jerry for opposite reasons. The irony is well-constructed, though the joke relies heavily on setup from earlier scenes.

jokes.text: Chris's envelope read by Ron: 'I hoped to be able to engage you in the process. And by that measure I succeeded.' / Ron's envelope: 'I predicted I would learn nothing from this process. Mission accomplished.'
jokes.setup: The seminar ends; they open their sealed envelopes containing what they hoped to gain
jokes.punchline: Both men's goals were achieved — Chris succeeded at the lowest possible bar (engagement) while Ron succeeded at complete non-learning — making both simultaneously right and both slightly ridiculous
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant resolution — both men are correct on their own terms, which means the entire exercise was pointless and successful simultaneously. 'Mission accomplished' from Ron is a perfect deadpan button. The parallel structure works well.

jokes.text: April's sealed envelope reveals her plan: 'I will pit Ron and Chris against each other. They'll argue about dumb stuff that doesn't matter, and I will bail. Then I'll steal $20 from Chris's wallet and buy pizza with Andy. And I'll also steal Ron's watch, just for fun.'
jokes.setup: Everyone opens their sealed envelopes — but April isn't there
jokes.punchline: April's envelope reveals she had the entire episode plotted from the opening — including robbing both men — while they were busy arguing about motivation theory
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and a contender for one of the best Parks gags in the run. The reveal works on multiple levels: (1) April had the plot mapped out at the start of the seminar; (2) both Ron and Chris's 'battle for her soul' was completely irrelevant to April; (3) the petty theft details are perfectly graded — $20 for pizza with Andy (practical) vs. stealing Ron's watch 'just for fun' (pure chaos). The escalation from planned to petty to chaotic is perfectly structured. The meta-element (the viewer has watched the whole storyline not knowing April was running it the whole time) adds enormous rewatch value. The line 'just for fun' is the perfect kicker — it's not about gain, it's about April being April. This absolutely justifies 9+.

jokes.text: Ron and Chris, reading April's letter in unison, both conclude she'll be a fine manager: 'I think April will be a fine manager.' / 'I agree.'
jokes.setup: April's plan to rob and abandon both of them has just been revealed
jokes.punchline: Both men — despite being robbed — immediately agree she'll make a fine manager, which is simultaneously the correct conclusion and completely absurd given the context
jokes.explanation: The button to April's envelope reveal — both men admitting they've been outplayed and that this proves she's management material — is a beautifully economical joke. Their shared conclusion functions as both sincere character insight and comedic capitulation. The irony (being robbed = management training complete) is well-earned.

jokes.text: Ron talking head: 'It's my favorite kind of battle. Two men enter, one me leaves.'
jokes.setup: Ron reflects on the seminar outcome
jokes.punchline: Twisting the Thunderdome 'two men enter, one man leaves' formula to 'two men enter, one me leaves' — Ron's narcissistic certainty that he always emerges as himself, unchanged and victorious
jokes.explanation: An exceptional line — the 'two men enter, one me leaves' construction is a masterclass in economical wordplay with character integration. The Thunderdome reference is well-known enough to land, but the 'one me' twist is genuinely novel and says something profound about Ron: he doesn't just win, he remains completely himself. Pure Ron Swanson philosophy distilled into seven words. This is comparable to the calibration anchor jokes in economy and quotability. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie receives the waffle iron and is told this will be the last Breakfast Day and Waffle Day. Leslie: 'Wait, what? Oh, my God. You're both dying.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann give Leslie the joint waffle iron present and announce they can't keep up with the anniversary celebrations
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate conclusion — upon being told something is 'the last' of something — is that both of them are terminally ill. It reveals both her anxiety and her drama
jokes.explanation: Leslie jumping to 'you're both dying' is a perfectly character-specific reaction — the most catastrophic possible interpretation, delivered with total conviction. The economy is good and the character integration is excellent. High quotability.

jokes.text: Ann and Ben announce they're canceling Breakfast Day and Waffle Day. Leslie: 'Oh, my God. You're both dying.'
jokes.setup: Ann and Ben say this will be the last Breakfast Day and Waffle Day
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate catastrophic interpretation of them stopping a holiday is that they must be terminally ill
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Leslie's logic — if two people simultaneously announce they're stopping something, they must be dying — is perfectly her: her anniversaries are such a central part of her worldview that canceling one is literally unimaginable except in the context of death. 'You're both dying' is direct, surprising, and completely in character. Strong delivery moment.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm no better at them than you are.' / Ben: 'That's ridiculous, I'm so much better.' / Leslie: 'Point taken.'
jokes.setup: Ben says they can't keep up because Leslie is so good at anniversaries
jokes.punchline: Leslie denies being better at anniversaries; Ben flatly contradicts her; Leslie immediately concedes — the speed of her capitulation reveals she knows it's true
jokes.explanation: 'Point taken' as instant capitulation is a great three-beat joke. The structure (denial / contradiction / immediate concession) is efficient and the character integration is strong — Leslie's self-awareness about her own excessive gift-giving is endearing.

jokes.text: 'What about Ann Month and Ben Month?' / 'How about a week?' / 'Fine.' [Ben talking head: 'We went in with a day, figuring she'd counter with a month. We were fine with a week.']
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann propose one 'Ann Day' and one 'Ben Day' as a compromise
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately counters with months; they negotiate to weeks; Ben's talking head reveals their negotiating strategy — 'we went in with a day, figuring she'd counter with a month' — confirming they expected this outcome
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke — Ben's talking head reveal that they planned for Leslie's counter-offer shows that knowing Leslie means building her escalation into your negotiations. It's both funny and sweet. The strategy of 'going in with a day' to land on a week is excellent character comedy. Strong running-gag resolution.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'But there will be a third week. It will be called Friend Week. It will be commemorating this week, the week that my two best friends became each other's best friends. I have a Friend Week present for you right now.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann have successfully negotiated their anniversary situation down to one week each
jokes.punchline: Leslie has already created a THIRD week — 'Friend Week' — commemorating the resolution of the anniversary negotiation, complete with presents already prepared. The meta-recursion: she's creating a new anniversary about reducing anniversaries
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode button for the Ben/Ann/Leslie storyline. The joke works because it's entirely inevitable given Leslie's character — of course she would create an anniversary about reducing anniversaries. The meta-recursion is structurally elegant, and 'I have a Friend Week present for you right now' (meaning she prepped it before the negotiation even ended) reveals the depth of her planning. Deeply character-integrated and a warm, funny way to close the emotional storyline. Justifies 8+.

tmdb_overview: Leslie works to get rid of outdated laws from the original town charter. April and Ron receive management training from Chris. Ben finds himself in a bidding war against Ann to win a present for Leslie.
insight: Leslie's constitutional amendment crusade fuels 55 jokes at a brisk 2-per-minute pace.
